## Styling data products people actually want to use

Shelby Level

Reporting & Analytics Analyst III

## Trust is an Emotional Gatekeeper {auto-animate=true}

::: notes
But we often overlook the other three dimensions: Quality & Design, Familiarity, and Personal Intuition, dismissing them as "superficial styling." However, these are the emotional and cognitive gatekeepers that can make or break whether someone trusts our work.

* Data Accuracy
* Source & Intent

* Execution & Aesthetics
* Psychological Alignment
* *Status: Often dismissed as "superficial styling."*

* **Aesthetics**
* **Visual Elements**
* **Professional Finish**

* **With Source**
* Reduces cognitive load
* Visual recognition
:::

## The Takeaway: Design Earns the Right to be Read

::: {.takeaway-wrap}

::: {.takeaway-quote}
"Data integrity builds the truth, but quality and design build the *bridge* to that truth."
:::

::: {.takeaway-list}
* **Without Quality:** Excellent data is dismissed as amateurish or suspicious.
* **Without Familiarity:** Complex data induces anxiety and cognitive rejection.
* **Without Personal Intuition:** The user lacks the raw confidence to act on your insights.
:::

:::

::: notes
The "Hard" Metrics (The Baseline): Data Integrity, Source, and Intent are what data professionals focus 99% of their time on. They are required, but they are invisible if the user rejects the chart upfront.

The "Soft" Metrics (The Gatekeepers): Quality, Familiarity, and Personal Intuition act as the emotional and cognitive gatekeeper. If a chart looks unprofessional or unfamiliar, viewers experience friction and judge it as untrustworthy before they even read a single data point.
:::

---

This is one of the easiest mistakes to make. We have a palette with six colors, so naturally we want to use all six colors.

Now every bar is bright, every card is competing for attention, and the audience has to decide where to begin.

Most of the time, color works better when we use less of it and reserve the strongest contrast for the point that matters most.

Here, I have made the decision for the audience of where to focus their attention.

# The uncomfortable truth

## Users judge the product before they read the insight

::: notes

People evaluate trustworthiness, usability, and professionalism almost instantly.

The visual experience becomes part of the analytical experience.

That may not feel fair, but it's reality.

:::

---

# The default look has a cost

- Feels unfinished
- Reduces confidence
- Lowers adoption
- Makes great analysis easier to ignore

::: notes

We've all built something that worked perfectly.

And then received little engagement.

Sometimes the issue isn't the analysis.

It's the experience surrounding the analysis.

:::

## Most of us are not CSS experts

# Why themes work

## They solve consistency for you

- Typography
- Spacing
- Color hierarchy
- Component styling
- Visual rhythm

::: notes

Consistency is one of the hardest things to create manually.

Themes provide consistency automatically.

:::

---

# But themes aren't enough

## Eventually everything starts looking the same

::: notes

Bootswatch is a great starting point.

But organizations and teams often need something more recognizable.

That's where brand.yml enters the picture.

:::

---

# Meet brand.yml

## Store design decisions in YAML

```yaml
meta:
  name: My Organization

color:
  primary: "#006699"

typography:
  fonts:
    - family: Source Sans Pro
```

::: notes

The key idea:

Design decisions become configuration rather than CSS.

:::

---

# What can brand.yml control?

- Colors
- Typography
- Logos
- Links
- Brand identity
- Reusable themes

::: notes

Think of brand.yml as a central source of truth.

:::

```{shinylive-r}
#| standalone: true

library(shiny)

# 1. User Interface (UI) - Defines how the app looks
ui <- fluidPage(
  titlePanel("Basic Shiny App Example"),

  sidebarLayout(
    sidebarPanel(
      # Input widget: A slider to select number of bins
      sliderInput(
        inputId = "bins",
        label = "Number of bins:",
        min = 1,
        max = 50,
        value = 30
      )
    ),

    mainPanel(
      # Output placeholder: Displays the generated plot
      plotOutput(outputId = "distPlot")
    )
  )
)

# 2. Server Logic - Defines how the app calculates outputs
server <- function(input, output) {
  # Reactive expression to render the plot based on user input
  output$distPlot <- renderPlot({
    # Use built-in Old Faithful geyser data
    x <- faithful$waiting
    bins <- seq(min(x), max(x), length.out = input$bins + 1)

    # Draw the histogram
    hist(
      x,
      breaks = bins,
      col = "#75AADB",
      border = "white",
      xlab = "Waiting time to next eruption (in mins)",
      main = "Histogram of Waiting Times"
    )
  })
}

# 3. Combine UI and Server into an App
shinyApp(ui = ui, server = server)
```
